lesson.title: Gas Lines and Stagflation: The Economic Crisis of the 1970s
lesson.summary: Twice in the 1970s, turmoil in the Middle East sent oil prices soaring and left Americans waiting in long lines at gas stations, while the economy suffered from a baffling new combination of high inflation and high unemployment that economists called stagflation.
lesson.body:
For much of the twentieth century, American economists had assumed that inflation and unemployment moved in opposite directions, so that a government could fight one only by tolerating more of the other. The 1970s shattered that assumption. During the Ford and Carter administrations, the country experienced stagflation, a combination of persistently high inflation, slow economic growth, and elevated unemployment happening all at once, a pattern that standard economic theory of the time struggled to explain.

Part of the story began even before the oil shocks, with changes to how money itself worked. In August 1971, President Nixon ended the direct convertibility of the U.S. dollar into gold, effectively taking the country off the international gold standard that had structured the global monetary system since the end of World War II. Supporters of the older system had argued that tying currency to gold restrained governments from printing too much money, and critics of the change argued that the shift to a purely fiat dollar, combined with heavy government spending in the late 1960s and early 1970s, helped set the stage for the inflation that followed.

The most visible trigger came in October 1973, when the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, led by its Arab members, imposed an oil embargo against the United States and other nations that had supported Israel during the Yom Kippur War. The embargo, combined with production cuts, roughly quadrupled the price of oil within months and produced long lines at American gas stations, with some states rationing sales by license plate number on odd and even days. A second oil shock followed in 1979, when the Iranian Revolution disrupted oil production and prices spiked again, deepening the economic troubles the country still had not solved from the first crisis.

The combination of expensive oil, an economy dependent on cheap energy, and a monetary system no longer anchored by gold pushed inflation to painful levels, with prices at times rising by well over ten percent a year, even as unemployment also climbed. The Federal Reserve, under chairman Arthur Burns for most of the decade, was reluctant to raise interest rates high enough to break inflation for fear of worsening unemployment, which allowed the problem to persist for years. It would take a change in Federal Reserve leadership at the end of the decade, and a new president willing to accept short term economic pain, to finally bring inflation back under control, a story that connects directly to the Reagan Revolution that followed.
